---
title: "Trait-gradient analysis"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

The trait-gradient analysis of Ackerly & Cornwell (2007) places each species along the
gradient defined by the mean trait of the communities it lives in. The species mean
\(\bar t_i\) splits into \(\beta_i\), the mean of the communities of the species, and
\(\alpha_i = \bar t_i - \beta_i\), its difference from the species it co-occurs with. The
gradient is built from the trait itself, so no environmental variable has to be chosen
beforehand. \(\beta\) measures where a species sorts among communities, and \(\alpha\)
measures how it differs within them.

`trait_gradient()` follows the original analysis with three changes, described in its help
page: site means leave out the focal species, the weights of site means and of species means
are chosen apart, and the tests use a null model with fixed margins and a phylogenetic model
that carries the sampling error of each value. The results below are simulated.

```{r}
library(comdynamite)

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(30)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(25), species_traits(tree, lambda = 1),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 5, local_adaptation = 0.5, intraspecific_sd = 1)
tg <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance")
tg
```

## The gradient

Each grey point is a population, at the mean of its site without the species itself. Lines
are the slopes of species over the range of their sites, and large points are the species
means at \((\beta_i, \bar t_i)\). Species above the dashed line have positive \(\alpha\):
they carry larger values than the species they live with.

```{r}
plot(tg)
```

## Leaving the focal species out

With the focal species inside the site means, \(\beta_i\) contains \(\bar t_i\), and the
more so the fewer species share its sites. The original \(\beta\) is pulled toward the mean
of the species itself; below are the species where the two versions differ most.

```{r}
original <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance", leave_one_out = FALSE)
both <- data.frame(species = tg$species$species, mean = tg$species$mean,
                   beta = tg$species$beta, beta_original = original$species$beta)
head(both[order(-abs(both$beta - both$beta_original)), ])
```

The raw correlation of \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) is not readable on its own under either
version, because \(\alpha = \bar t - \beta\): read it against a null model, as below. In
simulations without trait sorting, the curveball test of the correlation rejected in 49% of
replicates with the original site means and in 5% with the leave-one-out means.

## Weights

Abundance weights let the dominant species set the gradient. `trait_gradient_weights()` runs
the four combinations of weights for sites and species and correlates them with the first.

```{r}
trait_gradient_weights(ind, abundance = "abundance")$correlation
```

## Null models

`trait_gradient_test()` exchanges the trait means of species among species and keeps the
communities as observed, which tests whether species with similar traits live in similar
communities.

```{r}
test <- trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 199)
test
plot(test)
```

The curveball null moves species among sites instead, keeping the richness of every site and
the number of sites of every species. It also breaks the turnover of species along the
gradient, so its tests of the variances reject whenever composition changes among sites; use
it for the correlation of \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) only. The help page of
`trait_gradient_test()` gives the error rates of both nulls in simulations.

```{r}
trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 199, null = "curveball")$statistics[1, ]
```

When niches are conserved, a trait that merely carries the same phylogenetic structure looks
sorted along the gradient under the exchange of means among all species. The phylogenetic
permutations of Lapointe & Garland (2001) exchange means preferably among relatives; `phylo_k`
closer to 1 keeps exchanges closer in the tree.

```{r}
trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 199, null = "phylo", tree = tree)
```

## Phylogeny

`trait_gradient_phylo()` asks whether \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and the species mean are
conserved. Each value has a bootstrap standard error, added to the covariance of the model,
so a species seen in few sites does not pass for fast evolution.

```{r}
ph <- trait_gradient_phylo(tg, tree, n_boot = 199)
ph
```

In this simulation the optima evolve by Brownian motion (`lambda = 1`), so \(\beta\), which
follows the optima, should prefer Brownian motion over the model without phylogeny. A fit of
the OU process with its strength at a bound is marked in `at_bound`: at the lower bound it is
Brownian motion.

## A Bayesian model with latent beta

`trait_gradient_phylo()` first computes \(\beta\) and then models it with a standard error.
`trait_gradient_brms()` instead fits one bivariate model in which \(\beta\) and the species
mean are latent species effects, with a phylogenetic and a non-phylogenetic part, estimated
from every site of every species. The phylogenetic share \(\lambda\) of \(\beta\),
\(\alpha\) and the mean comes with a credible interval. It needs brms, and many species:
with about 20 species the chains do not separate the two parts, and even with 40 they mix
poorly when \(\beta\) has no phylogenetic signal. Abundance weights make the posterior too
narrow, so the model below uses occurrence weights for species.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tg_occ <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance", species_weights = "occurrence")
bayes <- trait_gradient_brms(tg_occ, tree, chains = 4, cores = 4)
bayes$diagnostics   # R-hat, effective sample sizes, divergent transitions
bayes$signal
bayesplot::pp_check(bayes, resp = "sitemean")
# an OU structure with the strength fitted to beta by trait_gradient_phylo()
a <- ph$models$a[ph$models$response == "beta" & ph$models$model == "OU"]
ou <- trait_gradient_brms(tg_occ, tree, ou_alpha = a, chains = 4, cores = 4)
# cross-validation one response at a time, since the two are fitted to different rows
brms::loo_compare(brms::loo(bayes$fit, resp = "sitemean"), brms::loo(ou$fit, resp = "sitemean"))
```

Lapointe, F.-J., & Garland, T., Jr. (2001). A generalized permutation model for the analysis
of cross-species data. *Journal of Classification*, 18, 109–127.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s00357-001-0007-0

*Nature Communications*, 5, 4114. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5114
